program.title: Program
program.short: A program is a set of written instructions that a computer carries out in order, one step after another.
program.body:
A computer does nothing on its own. It follows instructions. A program is a set of those instructions, written as text by a person. The computer carries them out in order, one after another, very fast.

Think of a recipe. It lists steps such as "heat the pan" and "add two eggs", and the cook does them in order. A program is a recipe for a computer. The difference is that a computer does exactly what the text says, even when the text has a mistake in it.

A program's text lives in files (see [[source-file|source file]]), written in a [[python|programming language]]. A pull request changes some of those files. To review it, you read the changed instructions and ask what the computer will now do differently.

The examples in this library are short Python programs, because Python reads close to plain English.

example.title: Three instructions, run in order
example.code:
price = 20
total = price * 3
print(f'Three tickets cost {total}.')
notes: Store the number 20 under the name price.
Multiply it by 3 and store the result, 60, under the name total.
Show the text "Three tickets cost 60." on the screen. The computer runs this line last because it comes last.

python.title: Python
python.short: Python is a popular programming language. A program called the interpreter reads Python text and carries it out.
python.body:
People write [[program|programs]] in a programming language, a small language with strict rules that a computer can follow without guessing. Python is one of the most widely used. JavaScript, TypeScript, Java and Go are others. They differ in punctuation and in details, but most of the ideas in these lessons carry across.

A computer's chip cannot read Python text directly. Another program, the Python interpreter, reads the text and carries out each instruction.

Python's designers made it read almost like English. if not items: means "if there are no items". Python also uses the spaces at the start of a line to show which lines belong together (see [[indentation|indentation]]). Many other languages use curly braces for that.

The examples in this library use Python. The ideas behind them, such as values, loops, functions and errors, exist in almost every language.

example.title: Python reads almost like English
notes: Take the list of items out of the cart. If the cart has none, use an empty list.
Ask a yes/no question. Python reads it almost like English, "if there are no items".
Only in that case, set the message. The 4 spaces at the start mark this line as part of the if.

source-file.title: Source file and module
source-file.short: A source file is a text file of program code, such as a .py file. In Python, each such file is also a module that other files can use.
source-file.body:
A [[program|program's]] text is saved in files, like any document. Python files end in .py, JavaScript files in .js. A file that holds program text is called a source file, because it is the source the program is made from.

Large programs are split across many files, each with one job. A small web shop might keep its pricing rules in pricing.py, its database code in storage.py and its web pages in views.py.

In Python, every .py file is also a module, a file whose names other files can borrow. A module's name is its file name without .py. views.py can borrow the [[function|function]] total_price from pricing.py with an [[module-import|import]] line.

Splitting code this way keeps each file small enough to read, and a change usually touches only a few files. When you read a pull request's [[diff|diff]], the first thing it shows is which files changed.

example.title: One module borrowing from two others
example.code:
# shop/views.py
from .pricing import total_price
from .storage import load_cart, save_order
notes: A comment naming the file. The lines below sit at the top of views.py.
Borrow the function total_price from pricing.py in the same folder.
Borrow two functions from storage.py.

statement.title: Line and statement
statement.short: A statement is one complete instruction. Python usually puts one statement on each line and runs them from top to bottom.
statement.body:
A statement is one complete instruction, like one step in a recipe. In [[python|Python]] each statement normally sits on its own line. The interpreter runs the first line, then the second, then the third, from top to bottom. Some statements make it jump instead. A [[for-loop|loop]] repeats lines, and an [[if|if]] skips them.

Some statements store a value, like count = 0. Some do something, like print('Saved.'). Some make a decision, like if count > 10:.

A long statement can spread over several lines when it sits inside brackets. Python treats the statement as unfinished until the brackets close.

Order matters. Moving a line up or down can change what a program does even when no word in it changes. If one line deletes a file and a later line reads it, the program fails. Swapping the two lines fixes it. In a [[diff|diff]], watch for lines that moved.

example.title: Four statements, run top to bottom
example.code:
order_id = 1042
print('Saving order...')
items = []
total = 0
notes: Statement 1. Store the order number.
Statement 2. Show a status message on the screen.
Statement 3. Start an empty list that will collect the order's items.
Statement 4. Start the running total at 0. Python runs these four lines in this order, top to bottom.

comment.title: Comment and docstring
comment.short: A comment is a note for human readers, after a # sign. A docstring is a description in triple quotes. Python runs neither.
comment.body:
Computers run code, and people read it. A comment is a note for the people. In Python a comment starts with # and runs to the end of the line. The interpreter skips it.

A docstring is a longer description in triple quotes ("""..."""), placed as the first [[statement|statement]] inside a [[function|function]], a [[class|class]] or a file. It says what that piece of code is for. Editors can show docstrings as help text, but they do not change what the program does.

Good comments explain why, because the code already shows what. "Retry 3 times because the payment service drops about 1 request in 200" helps the next reader. "Add 1 to count" does not.

The computer never checks a comment against the code. A comment can promise a time limit that no line enforces. When a review finds a comment and code that disagree, one of them is wrong.

example.title: Comments, a docstring and the code they describe
example.code:
# Give up on the payment service after this many seconds.
# Most replies arrive in under 2 seconds.
PAYMENT_TIMEOUT_S = 10

def order_key(user_id, n):
    """Build the storage key for a user's nth order."""
    return f'user-{user_id}.order-{n}'
notes: A comment. Python skips it. It tells the reader what the number below means.
The comment continues on a second line, which also starts with #.
Real code. Store 10 under the name PAYMENT_TIMEOUT_S.
Start a function named order_key (the def lesson explains this line).
A docstring. It describes the function in one sentence and does nothing when the program runs.
The real work. Build a key such as user-7.order-2 and hand it back.

indentation.title: Indentation
indentation.short: Indentation is the spaces at the start of a line. Python uses them to group lines into blocks, 4 spaces per level.
indentation.body:
Indentation means the spaces at the start of a line. In most writing it only makes text look tidy. In Python it changes the meaning. Lines indented under another line form a block that belongs to that line.

A line that ends with a colon, such as if total > 100: or for item in cart:, opens a block. Every following line that is indented further belongs to it. The block ends at the first line that moves back to the left. The standard is 4 spaces per level.

Because the spaces carry meaning, moving one line left or right can change what a program does. A line inside an [[if|if]] block runs only when the condition holds. Moved 4 spaces to the left, it runs every time. In a [[diff|diff]], a line whose only change is its indentation can still be a real change.

Many other languages mark blocks with curly braces instead, and their indentation is only for readers.

example.title: Blocks inside blocks
notes: Start a loop over every order. The colon at the end opens a block.
Indented 4 spaces, so it is inside the first loop. It starts a second loop over that order's items.
Indented 8 spaces, so it runs once for every item. It reads the item's name.
Also 8 spaces. Add one line of text, such as "- lamp", to the list.
Back at the left edge. This line is outside both loops, so it runs once, after they finish. It joins all the lines into one text.

error-message.title: Error message and traceback
error-message.short: When a program crashes, Python prints a traceback, the chain of calls it was in. The last line names the error and what went wrong.
error-message.body:
When Python reaches a line it cannot carry out, it stops and reports an error. The report is called a traceback. It lists the chain of places the [[program|program]] was in, from the outermost down to the exact line that failed. Read the last line first. It gives the error's type and a short message.

AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get' says the code asked a piece of text for an action that text does not have. KeyError: 'price' says the code looked up an entry named price that did not exist.

Python calls these errors [[exception|exceptions]]. A program can catch an exception and carry on instead of crashing (see [[try-except|try and except]]). Each kind has a fixed name, so programmers can search for it and write [[test|tests]] that expect it.

A bug report often starts with a traceback. A good fix explains why that line failed, not only how to stop the message.

example.title: A crash and its traceback
example.code:
items = ['lamp, 2']
for item in items:
    name = item.get('name')
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "orders.py", line 3, in <module>
# AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'
notes: A list with one item written as plain text, where the code expects a dictionary with named parts.
Go through each item in the list.
Ask the item for its "name" entry. Text has no .get action, so Python stops here with an error.
The traceback Python prints starts with this header line.
It names the file, the line number and where the code was running. <module> means the top level of the file.
The last line names the error type, AttributeError, and says what went wrong. Read this line first.

value.title: Value
value.short: A value is one piece of data a program works with, such as the number 80, the text 'hello' or True.
value.body:
Programs work with data. A single piece of data is a value. The number 80 is a value. The text 'hello' is a value. True is a value. Values are what a [[program|program]] stores, compares, sends and shows.

Every value has a type, which says what kind of thing it is and what you can do with it. You can add two [[number|numbers]]. You can turn [[string|text]] into capitals. You cannot add a number to text, and Python stops with an [[error-message|error]] if you try. The simple types are numbers, strings (text), [[boolean|True and False]] and [[none|None]]. Larger values hold other values, such as [[list|lists]] and [[dict|dictionaries]].

A value typed straight into the code, like 30 in timeout = 30, is called a literal. Most values in a running program are not typed in. They arrive from somewhere else, such as a user's form, a file or another program's reply.

Many bugs are about values of the wrong type. A form sends the text "5" where the code expects the number 5, or the text "false" where it expects the yes/no value False.

example.title: Five values of different types
example.code:
80
'hello'
True
None
['lamp', 'desk']
notes: A number.
A string, which is text. The quotes mark where it starts and ends.
A boolean, one of the two yes/no values.
None, Python's value for "nothing here".
A list, one value that holds two other values in order.

variable.title: Variable
variable.short: A variable is a name that points at a value. You create or change it with a single =, as in limit = 80.
variable.body:
A variable is a name that points at a [[value|value]]. Think of a sticky label on a jar. The label is the name, and the jar's contents are the value. You attach the label with a single equals sign, as in limit = 80.

That line is an assignment. It does not claim that limit equals 80, as it would in maths. It means "make the name limit point at 80". Later lines can write limit instead of 80, and Python looks up the value each time.

A variable can be pointed at a new value later. Python works out the right side of = first, then moves the name to the result, so count = count + 1 adds one to the count.

Names use letters, digits and underscores, with no spaces. Python programmers write them in lower case with underscores, such as retry_count. A good name says what the value means, so a reader can follow the code without comments. In review, a name that no longer matches what its value holds is worth a comment.

example.title: Creating and re-pointing names
example.code:
notes = ''
city = 'Lisbon'
notes = 'Flight lands at 9.'
count = 0
count = count + 1
first = last = -1
notes: Create the variable notes and point it at empty text.
Create a second variable, city, holding one word.
Point notes at new text. The old empty text is forgotten.
Start a counter at 0.
Python works out count + 1 first, which is 1, then points count at it.
Two names at once. Both first and last point at -1, a common way to mean "not yet".

string.title: String (text)
string.short: A string is a piece of text in quotes, like 'hello'. You can measure it, cut pieces out of it and clean it up.
string.body:
A string is a [[value|value]] that holds text. You write it between single or double quotes, as in 'hello' or "hello". Python treats both the same. Text that spans several lines goes in triple quotes.

Strings come with tools. len(s) gives the number of characters. s.strip() gives a copy with spaces and line breaks removed from both ends. s.lower() gives a lower-case copy. s[:80] gives the first 80 characters (see [[index-slice|slicing]]).

A string never changes in place. Each of those tools makes a new string and leaves the old one as it was. That is why code writes answer = answer.strip().lower(), which points the [[variable|variable]] at the cleaned copy. Calling answer.strip() on its own line, without the =, throws the cleaned copy away. That is a common slip.

Much of what programs handle is text, such as file contents, web pages, messages and user input.

example.title: Measuring and cleaning text
example.code:
path = 'docs/intro.md'
len(path)
path.upper()
path[:4]
' YES '.strip().lower()
notes: Make a string holding a file path and name it path.
Count its characters. The result is 13.
Make an upper-case copy, 'DOCS/INTRO.MD'. path itself does not change.
Take the first 4 characters, 'docs'.
Remove the spaces at both ends, then lower-case it. The result is 'yes'.

number.title: Number
number.short: Python has whole numbers (int) and decimals (float). You can do arithmetic on them, including //, which divides and drops the remainder.
number.body:
Python has two everyday kinds of number. An int (integer) is a whole number, such as 8, -1 or 4000. A float is a number with a decimal point, such as 0.2 or 2.5. You write numbers without quotes. '80' in quotes is text, not a number.

You can do arithmetic with +, -, * and /. Ordinary division / always gives a float, so 10 / 4 is 2.5. Integer division // drops the part after the point, so 10 // 4 is 2. The [[operator|operators]] lesson lists the rest.

Floats are stored in binary, so some decimals cannot be exact. 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. That is why code that handles money often counts whole cents as ints. In review, a float used for money or compared with == is worth a question.

example.title: Splitting a budget
example.code:
budget = 1000
parts = 3
share = budget // parts
head = (share * 2) // 3
tail = share - head
price_cents = 1999
notes: A budget of 1,000 characters to share out.
Three parts of a message want a share.
Integer division. Each part gets 333 characters. Plain / would give 333.33.
Keep two thirds of a long text from its start. (333 * 2) // 3 is 222.
The rest, 111 characters, comes from its end.
Money as a whole number of cents, so there is no rounding error.

boolean.title: True and False
boolean.short: A boolean is one of two values, True or False. Comparisons produce them, and decisions in code depend on them.
boolean.body:
A boolean is a [[value|value]] that can only be True or False. In Python both start with a capital letter and have no quotes. With quotes, 'True' would be text that happens to spell the word.

Booleans answer yes/no questions. 5 > 3 produces True. len(items) < 10 produces True or False depending on the numbers (see [[comparison|comparison]]). Decisions in code, such as [[if|if]], go one way when the answer is True and another way when it is False.

Programmers often store a boolean in a [[variable|variable]] whose name reads like a yes/no question, such as is_paid or has_errors.

[[json|JSON]], a common format for sending data, writes the same two values in lower case, true and false. When data arrives as "paid": "false", with quotes, the value is a string, not a boolean. Code that treats it as a yes/no answer then goes wrong (see [[truthiness|truthiness]]).

example.title: Yes/no values
example.code:
is_paid = False
send_receipt = True
too_long = len('docs/intro.md') > 80
fits = not too_long
notes: A boolean variable. The order has not been paid.
Another one.
A comparison gives a boolean. 13 is not more than 80, so too_long is False.
not flips a boolean. fits becomes True.

none.title: None
none.short: None is Python's value for "nothing" or "missing". Functions return it to say there is no result.
none.body:
None is a special [[value|value]] that means "nothing here". It is not zero and it is not empty text. It stands for a missing value. Python has exactly one None, so code checks for it with is None or is not None.

Programs use None to say "no answer" or "not set". A [[function|function]] that finds nothing can hand back None. A setting that nobody filled in can start as None.

That habit has a trap. If a lookup returns None both for "not found" and for "found, and the stored value is None", the caller cannot tell the two apart. Code that needs the difference returns a separate marker for "not found", or raises an [[exception|exception]].

A second trap is a missing value that turns into a silent blank. If the caller replaces None with empty text, the user sees a gap and nobody learns that data was missing. A visible marker such as [missing: price] is easier to debug. [[json|JSON]] writes the same idea as null.

If so, hand back its price.
Otherwise hand back None, meaning "not found".
Ask for a product that is not there.

f-string.title: f-string
f-string.short: An f-string is text with an f before the opening quote. Python replaces anything in {curly braces} inside it with its value.
f-string.body:
Programs often build text from pieces. An f-string is a [[string|string]] with the letter f just before the opening quote. Inside it, anything in curly braces is worked out and dropped into the text. If n is 2, then f'page-{n}' becomes 'page-2'.

The braces can hold more than a name. f'Step {n + 1} of 5' does the sum first. f'{len(text)} chars' counts characters. {name!r} shows the value the way Python would write it, with its quotes. That helps in log messages, because empty text shows as '' instead of nothing.

Without f-strings you would glue pieces with + and turn numbers into text by hand, as in 'page-' + str(n). f-strings are shorter and easier to read.

A plain string with braces but no f in front is a common slip. 'page-{n}' stays exactly that text, braces and all.

example.title: Building keys and messages
example.code:
user_id = 7
n = 2
key = f'user-{user_id}.order-{n}'
step = 0
message = f'Step {step + 1} of 5'
name = ''
log_line = f'name={name!r}'
notes: A user's id number.
Their order number.
Build a storage key. The result is 'user-7.order-2'.
Counting in code often starts at 0.
The braces can hold a sum. The result is 'Step 1 of 5', the status line a person sees.
An empty name, as a bug might produce.
!r shows the quotes, so the result is name='' and the empty value is easy to spot.

operator.title: Operators
operator.short: Operators are symbols and words that combine values, like + and // for numbers, and/or/not for yes/no values, and in for membership.
operator.body:
An operator takes one or two [[value|values]] and produces a new one. The arithmetic operators work on [[number|numbers]]:

  • + adds, - subtracts and * multiplies.
  • / divides and gives a decimal. // divides and drops the remainder. % gives the remainder.
  • + also joins two strings, so 'page-' + '2' is 'page-2'.

Three word operators work on [[boolean|yes/no values]]. a and b is true only if both are true. a or b is true if either is. not a flips the answer. or has a useful habit. It gives back the first value that counts as true, so data.get('items') or [] means "the items, or an empty list if there are none" (see [[truthiness|truthiness]]).

The in operator asks whether something is inside a collection or a piece of text. 'error' in line is true if that word appears in line. status not in ('done', 'failed') is true if the status is neither of those two.

example.title: Operators at work
example.code:
10 // 4
10 % 4
'page-' + '2'
data.get('items') or []
'error' in 'error: disk full'
not True
notes: Integer division. The result is 2.
The remainder of the same division, 2.
Joining two strings gives 'page-2'.
If data has items, use them. If it has none, use an empty list instead.
in looks for the word inside the text. The result is True.
not flips True to False.

comparison.title: Comparison
comparison.short: Comparisons ask how two values relate, using == != < <= > >= and is. Each one answers True or False.
comparison.body:
A comparison asks a question about two values and answers with a [[boolean|boolean]]. The comparison operators are these:

  • == equal, and != not equal.
  • < less than, and <= less than or equal.
  • > greater than, and >= greater than or equal.
  • is asks whether both sides are the very same object. Programmers use it mostly with None, True and False.

Note the double equals. A single = stores a value in a [[variable|variable]]. A double == asks whether two values are equal.

== and is ask different questions. Python treats True as the number 1 in arithmetic, so 1 == True is True. But 1 and True are different objects, so 1 is True is False. Code that must accept only a real True can test value is True.

JavaScript has two equality operators. == converts types first, so '1' == 1 is true there. === compares without converting, and most JavaScript code uses it.

example.title: Asking questions about values
example.code:
len('docs/intro.md') <= 80
'user-7' != 'user-8'
paid = 1
paid == True
paid is True
v = None
v is None
notes: 13 characters is at most 80, so this is True.
Two different keys, so != gives True.
Suppose some data says paid is the number 1.
== says True, because Python counts True as 1.
is says False, because 1 is not the True object.
Set v to None.
is None is the standard way to check for None. The result is True.

truthiness.title: Truthiness
truthiness.short: Python treats empty text, 0, empty collections and None as false, and almost everything else as true, even the text 'false'.
truthiness.body:
An [[if|if]] statement needs a yes or a no. If you give it something that is not a [[boolean|boolean]], Python decides whether it counts as true or false. This is called truthiness. These count as false:

  • None and False
  • the number 0 (and 0.0)
  • empty text, ''
  • empty collections, such as [] (an empty [[list|list]]) and {} (an empty [[dict|dictionary]])

Everything else counts as true. That includes any text with at least one character in it, even '0', ' ' and 'false'. Programmers use this as a shortcut. if not items: means "if the list is empty or missing".

The shortcut goes wrong when text stands in for a yes/no value. If data arrives as "done": "false", with quotes, then if data['done']: sees a 5-letter string, which is truthy, and treats "not done" as done. The fix is to turn the text into a real boolean by its meaning first.

JavaScript has the same idea with one surprise. An empty array, [], counts as true there, so JavaScript code checks items.length === 0 instead.

example.title: Why the text 'false' counts as true
example.code:
bool('')
bool('false')
bool([])
bool(['lamp'])
done = 'false'
if done:
    print('treated as done')
done = done.strip().lower() == 'true'
notes: bool() shows how Python judges a value. Empty text is False.
Any non-empty text is True, even the word false.
An empty list is False.
A list with one item is True.
Some data sent the text 'false' instead of the value False.
Python asks whether 'false' is truthy. It is.
So this line runs, which is the bug.
The fix. Compare the cleaned text with 'true'. The result is the real boolean False.

list.title: List
list.short: A list is an ordered collection of values in square brackets. Positions count from 0, and append adds an item at the end.
list.body:
A list holds several [[value|values]] in order, inside square brackets, separated by commas. ['lamp', 'desk'] is a list of two strings. A list can hold any values, including other lists and [[dict|dictionaries]]. Order is kept, and the same item can appear twice. Other languages often call it an array.

Each item has a position, called its index, and counting starts at 0. items[0] is the first item. len(items) gives how many items there are. items.append(x) adds x at the end and changes the list in place. The [[index-slice|indexing and slicing]] lesson covers positions in more detail.

Python can also build a list from another in one line, which is called a list comprehension. [o['id'] for o in orders] makes a list of the order ids, one per order.

In review, watch for code that reads items[0] without checking that the list has an item. An empty list makes that line fail with an IndexError.

example.title: Working with a list of orders
example.code:
orders = [{'id': 1, 'total': 20}, {'id': 2, 'total': 35}]
len(orders)
orders[0]
lines = []
lines.append('order 1: paid')
ids = [o['id'] for o in orders]
notes: A list of two orders. Each order is a small dictionary.
How many orders? 2.
The first order, {'id': 1, 'total': 20}. Positions start at 0.
An empty list, ready to collect lines of text.
Add one line at the end. lines now has 1 item.
Build a new list of ids, [1, 2], one per order.

dict.title: Dictionary
dict.short: A dictionary stores values under keys, in {}. You look values up by key. .get(key, default) avoids a crash when the key is missing.
dict.body:
A dictionary (dict) stores [[value|values]] under names called keys. You write it in curly braces, with a colon between each key and its value, as in {'name': 'lamp', 'price': 25}. Other languages call the same thing a map, a hash or an object.

Think of a set of labelled drawers. To get something out, you name the drawer. item['price'] gives 25. item['color'] = 'red' puts a value in a drawer, and creates the drawer if it was not there.

Square brackets with a key that does not exist stop the program with a KeyError. item.get('size') is the safe version. It gives [[none|None]] when the key is missing. item.get('size', 'M') gives the second value, here 'M', instead. Code that reads data from outside, such as a web request, uses .get because any key might be missing.

.items() goes through every key and value in turn.

example.title: An order as a dictionary
example.code:
order = {'id': 7, 'paid': False, 'items': []}
order['paid']
order.get('note')
order.get('note', '')
order['note'] = 'Leave at the door.'
for k, v in order.items():
    print(k, v)
notes: A dictionary with three keys.
Look up the key paid. The result is False.
note is not there. .get returns None instead of crashing.
With a default, .get returns the empty text ''.
Add a new key, note.
Go through every key and value pair, in the order they were added.
Show each pair, such as paid False.

tuple.title: Tuple
tuple.short: A tuple is a fixed group of values in round brackets, like (x, y). Functions use tuples to hand back two things at once.
tuple.body:
A tuple is like a [[list|list]] that cannot change. You write it with round brackets, (order, problems), or often with commas alone, order, problems. Once it is made, you cannot add, remove or replace its items.

Programmers use a tuple for a small, fixed group where each position has a meaning, such as a pair of map coordinates, (38.7, -9.1).

Its most common job is handing back two results from a [[function|function]]. A function can end with return order, problems. The caller unpacks the pair into two [[variable|variables]] in one line, order, problems = check_order(data). The first name gets the first item and the second name gets the second.

Tuples also hold fixed sets of options, as in status in ('done', 'failed'). One detail trips people up. A tuple with one item needs a comma, ('done',). Without it, the brackets are only grouping, and ('done') is a plain string.

example.title: Returning and unpacking a pair
notes: A function that checks an order and reports what was wrong.

set.title: Set
set.short: A set is a collection with no duplicates and no order. Checking whether something is in a set is very fast.
set.body:
A set holds [[value|values]] with no repeats and no fixed order. You make an empty one with set(), or write values in curly braces, as in {'red', 'blue'}. Adding something that is already there does nothing.

Think of a guest list at a door. Each name appears once, and the main question is whether a person is on it. A set answers that question fast, even when it is large (the [[hash-table|hash table]] lesson explains how). Asking the same question of a [[list|list]] means checking the items one by one.

The common actions are s.add(x), s.discard(x), which removes x if present and does nothing otherwise, and the test x in s. set(items) turns a list into a set and drops its repeats.

A typical use is tracking what has already been handled, such as the files a program has opened, so it can close exactly those at the end. Because a set has no order, code that needs a stable order sorts it first.

example.title: Tracking which files are open
example.code:
opened = set()
opened.add('a.txt')
opened.add('a.txt')

sorted(opened)

index-slice.title: Indexing and slicing
index-slice.short: x[0] picks the first item and x[-1] the last. A slice like s[:80] takes a range, here the first 80 characters.
index-slice.body:
[[list|Lists]] and [[string|strings]] keep their items in order, so you can pick items by position with square brackets after the name. x[0] is the first item and x[1] the second. Negative numbers count from the end, so x[-1] is the last item.

A slice takes a range instead of one item. x[a:b] starts at position a and stops just before b. Leave out a to start at the beginning, or leave out b to run to the end. So s[:80] is the first 80 characters, and s[-40:] is the last 40. A slice never crashes when the text is shorter. It returns what there is. Slicing makes a new string or list and leaves the original as it was.

Code often slices to cut long text down to size. Keeping only the start can hide what matters. The last line of an error log usually names the error, so a cut that keeps both ends, s[:head] and s[-tail:], often works better (see [[budget|budgets and truncation]]).

example.title: Cutting the head and tail of a text
example.code:
value = 'ValueError: price must be a number'
value[0]
value[-1]
value[:10]
value[-6:]
head, tail = 10, 6
f'{value[:head]} ... {value[-tail:]}'
notes: A 34-character text, like the last line of an error log.
The first character, 'V'.
The last character, 'r'.
The first 10 characters, 'ValueError'.
The last 6 characters, 'number'.
Keep 10 characters from the start and 6 from the end.
The result is 'ValueError ... number', with the middle dropped.

json.title: JSON
json.short: JSON is a text format for data. json.loads turns JSON text into Python data, and json.dumps turns Python data back into JSON text.
json.body:
Programs often send data to each other as text. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the most common text format for that. It looks almost the same as Python's [[dict|dictionaries]] and [[list|lists]], as in {"paid": true, "items": ["lamp"]}.

The differences are small. JSON uses double quotes only. It writes true, false and null in lower case, where Python writes True, False and None. JSON calls a dictionary an object and a list an array.

Python's json module converts both ways. json.loads(text) reads JSON text and returns Python values. json.dumps(data) writes Python values out as JSON text. If the text is not valid JSON, json.loads stops with an error (see [[parsing|parsing]]).

Web APIs, configuration files and log tools all use JSON. Valid JSON can still hold the wrong shape, such as a string where the code expects an object, so careful code checks the shape after it parses.

example.title: From text to data and back
example.code:
import json
text = '{"paid": false, "items": [{"name": "lamp", "qty": 2}]}'
order = json.loads(text)
order['paid']
order['items'][0]['name']
json.dumps({'ok': True, 'id': 7})

The reverse direction. The result is the text {"ok": true, "id": 7}.

if.title: if, elif, else
if.short: if runs a block of code only when a condition is true. elif and else add other paths for when it is not.
if.body:
Programs make decisions. An if statement runs a block of lines only when a condition is true. You write if, the condition, a colon, and then the indented block. Python works out the condition. If it is true, or [[truthiness|truthy]], the block runs. If not, Python skips it.

else: adds a block for the other case. elif, short for "else if", adds more conditions, checked in order. Only the first block whose condition holds runs.

A common use is a guard, a check near the top that handles a bad or finished case and leaves early with [[return|return]]. Guards keep the main path of a function unindented and easy to read.

The order of an elif chain matters. Python counts True as a number, so a chain that asks "is it a number?" before "is it a boolean?" sends True down the number path. When you review a chain, ask whether an early branch catches cases meant for a later one.

for-loop.title: for loop
for-loop.short: A for loop runs the same block once for each item in a collection, such as each order in a list.
for-loop.body:
A for loop repeats a block of lines once per item in a collection. for order in orders: means "take each order in turn, name it order, and run the indented block". When the items run out, Python carries on with the first line after the block.

Think of sorting a stack of letters. You pick one up, deal with it, put it down and take the next, until the stack is empty.

range(n) gives the numbers 0, 1, 2 and so on up to n - 1, so a loop over it runs n times. for attempt in range(3): allows at most 3 attempts.

enumerate(items) gives each item together with its position, which helps when a message must say which item was wrong, as in items[2]. Loops can sit inside loops. The inner loop runs in full for every round of the outer one, so two loops over 1,000 items each run the inner block a million times.

example.title: A loop with a limit
example.code:
max_tries = 3
for attempt in range(max_tries):
    print(f'Attempt {attempt + 1}')
print('Giving up.')
notes: This code may try at most 3 times.
Repeat the block with attempt set to 0, then 1, then 2.
Runs three times. It shows Attempt 1, Attempt 2 and Attempt 3, one per round.
Not indented, so it runs once, after the loop ends.

while-loop.title: while loop
while-loop.short: A while loop repeats a block as long as a condition stays true, checking the condition before each round.
while-loop.body:
A while loop repeats its block as long as a condition is true. Python checks the condition, runs the block, checks again, and so on. When the condition turns false, Python moves on to the first line after the loop.

Use while when you do not know in advance how many rounds you need. A [[for-loop|for loop]] fits "once per item". A while loop fits "until this is done", like stirring until the sauce thickens.

The danger is a loop whose condition never becomes false. It runs forever and the program hangs. Every while loop needs something inside it that moves it toward the end. When you review one, find that line. If it sits inside an if, ask what happens on the rounds where the if is false.

A common pattern keeps a [[set|set]] of unfinished jobs and loops while pending:. Each round removes the jobs that finished, so the set shrinks and the loop ends.

notes: Two jobs are still running. A set holds them.

break-continue.title: break and continue
break-continue.short: break leaves a loop at once. continue skips the rest of the current round and starts the next one.
break-continue.body:
Sometimes a [[for-loop|loop]] should stop early, or skip part of a round. Python has two statements for this:

  • break leaves the loop at once. Python goes to the first line after the loop.
  • continue skips the rest of the current round and starts the next round, with the next item.

Both usually sit inside an [[if|if]], so they happen only in a certain situation. break fits "stop searching, I found it" or "stop, there is nothing left to do". continue fits "this item is bad, skip it and go on".

Skipping with continue keeps one malformed entry from throwing away the good ones. The code records the problem, then moves on to the next entry. When you review such a loop, check that the skipped item is reported somewhere, so it does not vanish without a trace.

example.title: Skipping a malformed entry
example.code:
problems, good = [], []
rows = ['lamp 25', {'name': 'desk', 'price': 120}]
for i, row in enumerate(rows):
    if not isinstance(row, dict):
        problems.append(f'rows[{i}] was not an object')
        continue
    good.append(row)
notes: Two empty lists, one for problems and one for good entries.

return.title: return
return.short: return hands a value back to the code that called the function, and ends the function on that line.
return.body:
A [[function|function]] often works something out for the code that called it. return hands that result back. When Python reaches a return line, the function stops at once, and the lines after it do not run.

The value after return becomes the value of the call. If area(3, 4) ends with return width * height, the call itself stands for 12, and the caller can store it in a [[variable|variable]]. A function with no return, or a bare return, hands back [[none|None]].

Because return ends the function, programmers use it for early exits. A function can return a short answer for a simple case at the top and do the full work below. It can also return two values at once as a [[tuple|tuple]], as in return order, problems.

The position of a return can decide a bug. Cleanup lines placed after a return never run on that path. Cleanup placed before it can delete data that the returned result still needs.

function.title: Function
function.short: A function is a named set of steps you can run whenever you need it. It takes inputs and usually hands back a result.
function.body:
A function is a named group of [[statement|statements]] that you can run again and again. You write the steps once and give them a name. After that, writing the name with brackets, as in total_price(cart), runs all the steps.

Think of a recipe card titled "Pancakes". It lists the steps, takes ingredients as its inputs and produces pancakes as its output. You can follow it any number of times, with different ingredients each time.

A function's inputs are called [[parameter|parameters]], and it usually hands back a result with [[return|return]]. Python comes with many functions, such as len(x), which counts the items in x. Programmers write their own with [[def|def]].

Splitting work into functions gives each piece one job, a name that says what it does, and a way to [[test|test]] it on its own. Most pull requests change the inside of one or two functions, so a walkthrough usually explains a change function by function.

example.title: One recipe, used three times
example.code:
def order_key(user_id, n):
    return f'user-{user_id}.order-{n}'

first = order_key(7, 1)
second = order_key(7, 2)
other = order_key(9, 1)
notes: Define a function named order_key with two inputs.
Its one step. Build the key text and hand it back.
Run it. first is 'user-7.order-1'.
Run it again with other inputs. second is 'user-7.order-2'.
And again. other is 'user-9.order-1'. One definition serves all three calls.

def.title: def
def.short: def is the keyword that creates a function. It gives the name, the inputs in brackets, and an indented block of steps.
def.body:
def, short for "define", creates a [[function|function]]. The line always has the same shape, as in def shorten(text, limit):. After def come the function's name, its inputs in round brackets separated by commas, and a colon.

The [[indentation|indented]] lines below form the function's body, the steps it runs. The body often starts with a docstring (see [[comment|comment and docstring]]) and often ends with [[return|return]].

Writing def does not run anything. It only stores the steps under the name. The steps run later, each time some code [[call|calls]] the function.

Real def lines often carry extra notes. def shorten(text: str, limit: int = 80) -> str: says what kind of value each input should be and that the function returns text (see [[type-hint|type hints]]). limit: int = 80 gives that input a default (see [[keyword-argument|default values]]).

example.title: A whole function, from def to return
example.code:
def keep_ends(text: str, limit: int) -> str:
    """Keep the start and end of text when it is longer than limit."""
    if len(text) <= limit:
        return text
    head = (limit * 2) // 3
    tail = limit - head
    return f'{text[:head]} ... {text[-tail:]} ({len(text)} chars)'
notes: def starts a new function named keep_ends with two inputs, text and limit.
The docstring says what the function does.
If the text is short enough...
...hand back the whole text, and stop.
Otherwise keep two thirds of the limit from the start...
...and the remaining third from the end.
Hand back the start, " ... ", the end, and the full length.

parameter.title: Parameter and argument
parameter.short: Parameters are the input names listed in a def. Arguments are the actual values you pass in when you call the function.
parameter.body:
A [[function|function]] usually needs inputs. The names listed in brackets in the def line are its parameters. Inside the function they work like [[variable|variables]]. The values you hand over when you run the function are the arguments.

In def order_key(user_id, n): the parameters are user_id and n. In the call order_key(7, 2) the arguments are 7 and 2. Python matches them by position, first argument to first parameter. Each call gets fresh parameters, so two calls with different arguments do not interfere.

A recipe that says "add the sugar" has a slot named sugar. Each time you cook, a real amount of sugar goes into that slot.

In a review, a removed parameter is worth a look. Every caller that still passes it will now fail. An added parameter needs a value from every caller, or a default (see [[keyword-argument|default values]]).

keyword-argument.title: Keyword argument and default value
keyword-argument.short: A keyword argument names its parameter in the call, as in limit=40. A default value is used when the caller leaves that parameter out.
keyword-argument.body:
Normally Python matches [[parameter|arguments to parameters]] by position. You can instead name the parameter in the call, as in shorten(text, limit=40). That is a keyword argument. It makes a call easier to read, and the order of named arguments does not matter.

A parameter can have a default value, written in the def line with =. In def shorten(text, limit=80):, a caller that does not mention limit gets 80. Defaults keep old callers working when a function gains a new input. A pull request can add a parameter with a default, and every existing call stays correct without a change.

A lone * in the parameter list makes callers pass every parameter after it by name. With def send(*, to, subject, body):, a caller has to write to=..., so it cannot swap the subject and the body by mistake.

Watch for one trap. A default such as items=[] is made once, when Python reads the def, and every call shares that one list. Use items=None and create the list inside.

call.title: Calling a function
call.short: Writing a function's name followed by brackets, like len(text), runs the function. The call then stands for the value it returns.
call.body:
Defining a [[function|function]] stores its steps. Calling it runs them. You call a function by writing its name followed by round brackets with the [[parameter|arguments]] inside, as in order_key(7, 2). A function with no inputs still needs the brackets, as in new_cart(). Without them, new_cart names the function and runs nothing.

When Python reaches a call, it jumps into the function, runs its body with the arguments in place, and comes back with the [[return|returned]] value. The call then stands for that value, so key = order_key(7, 2) stores 'user-7.order-2'.

Calls can be nested, and Python works from the inside out. In len(name.strip()) it runs strip first, then passes the result to len.

Calls chain across files. One function calls a second, which calls a third. A [[error-message|traceback]] lists exactly such a chain of calls, outermost first. To follow a change in a pull request, it helps to find who calls the changed function.

example.title: A chain of calls
example.code:
cart = load_cart(user_id)
total = total_price(cart)
order, problems = check_order(cart)
count = len(problems)
notes: Call load_cart to fetch the cart. Its returned value is stored in cart.
Call total_price on the cart. This line waits until the function returns.
Call check_order. It returns two values.
len is a call too. It returns how many problems there were.

scope.title: Scope
scope.short: Scope is where a name is visible. A name made inside a function exists only there. A top-level name is visible in the whole file.
scope.body:
A [[variable|variable]] name is not visible everywhere. Its scope is the part of the program where Python can find it.

  • A name created inside a [[function|function]], including its parameters, is local. It exists only while that call runs, and code outside the function cannot see it. Each call gets its own fresh copy.
  • A name created at the top level of a file, outside every function, is module-level, also called global. Every function in that [[source-file|module]] can read it.

A local name is like a whiteboard in a meeting room, wiped after each meeting. A module-level name is like a notice on the building's front door that everyone sees.

Settings usually live at module level, such as TIMEOUT_S = 30. Work in progress should stay local, so that two calls running at once cannot mix up each other's data (see [[shared-state|shared state]]). Tests can swap a module-level name for a short time, for example to make a timeout shorter (see [[fixture|monkeypatch]]).

example.title: Local and module-level names
example.code:
TIMEOUT_S = 30

def handle_request():
    notes = ''
    print(TIMEOUT_S)

handle_request()
print(notes)

A function.

inner-function.title: Inner function and closure
inner-function.short: An inner function is a def inside another def. It can use the outer function's variables, which makes it a closure.
inner-function.body:
You can write a def inside another [[function|function]]. The result is an inner function. It exists only inside the outer function, so nothing else in the file can call it by name.

An inner function can read the outer function's local [[variable|variables]] (see [[scope|scope]]). It keeps that access even when it is handed to other code to run later. A function that keeps access to the variables around it is called a closure. This saves passing the same values in again and again.

A common use is a small job handed to other code, such as a [[thread-pool|pool of worker threads]]. The inner function takes only the item to work on, and finds everything else, such as a shared results table, in the outer function.

In review, notice which outer variables an inner function changes. If several threads run it at once, they all change the same variables.

lambda.title: lambda
lambda.short: lambda makes a small function in one line without giving it a name, such as lambda x: x * 2.
lambda.body:
lambda makes a short [[function|function]] inside one expression, with no def line and no name. lambda x: x * 2 is a function that takes x and returns x * 2. The part before the colon lists the [[parameter|parameters]], and the part after it is the value it returns. A lambda can hold only that one expression.

Programmers use a lambda when some code needs a function as an input and the function is too small to deserve a name. sorted(orders, key=lambda o: o['total']) sorts orders by their total.

Tests use lambdas as small stand-ins (see [[fake|fakes]]). send_email = lambda *args: None replaces a real email call with one that does nothing. A fake clock can be lambda: clock.now, a function that returns whatever time the test has set.

example.title: A pretend clock built with a lambda
example.code:
clock = SimpleNamespace(now=0.0)
fake_time = SimpleNamespace(monotonic=lambda: clock.now)
fake_time.monotonic()
clock.now = 11.0
fake_time.monotonic()
notes: An object that holds one number, now, the time on a pretend clock. It starts at 0.
A stand-in for Python's time module. Its monotonic is a lambda with no inputs that returns clock.now.
Returns 0.0.
The test moves the clock forward by hand, 11 seconds.
Returns 11.0. The lambda reads clock.now each time it is called, so it sees the new value.

module-import.title: import
module-import.short: import brings names from another module into this file. from .pricing import total reads total from pricing.py in the same folder.
module-import.body:
A [[source-file|module]] can use code from other modules. An import line brings it in. There are two common shapes:

  • import json loads the whole json module. You then write json.loads(...), with the module's name in front.
  • from typing import Any takes the listed names out of a module, so you can write Any directly.

as renames on the way in. from .pricing import total as order_total brings in total under the name order_total, which keeps it apart from other things called total.

The dot in .pricing makes it a relative import. It means "the module named pricing in the same folder as this file". Without the dot, Python looks in its installed libraries and the project's top-level folders.

Python runs a module's top-level code the first time anything imports it, then reuses it. Imports sit at the top of a file, so a reader sees at once what the file depends on. A new import in a [[diff|diff]] tells you the file now depends on something new.

example.title: The imports at the top of a file
example.code:
import json
from typing import Any

import requests
from .pricing import total as order_total
from .storage import load_cart, save_order
notes: Load Python's json module. The code later calls json.loads(...).
Take one name from Python's typing module. It is used in type hints.
Load an installed library, requests, which makes web requests.

package.title: Package
package.short: A package is a folder of Python modules with an __init__.py file. Dotted names like shop.payments point into it.
package.body:
A [[module-import|module]] is one file. A package is a folder that groups related modules. Python treats a folder as a package when it contains a file named __init__.py. Python runs that file the first time any code imports the package, and it often just lists what the package offers.

Packages can hold other packages, which gives dotted names. shop.payments.cards means the module cards inside the folder payments inside the folder shop. Each dot is one folder level.

Test folders can be packages too. When two test folders each hold a file with the same name, such as test_client.py, [[pytest|pytest]] can load both only when each folder is its own package. A pull request that adds an empty __init__.py to a test folder may be fixing that clash.

The word package has a second meaning. A library you install, for example with pip install requests, is also called a package.

example.title: A package's __init__ file
example.code:
# shop/payments/__init__.py
from .cards import charge_card
from .refunds import refund

__all__ = ['charge_card', 'refund']
notes: A comment with the file's path. This is the package's __init__.py.
Bring charge_card in from cards.py in the same folder.
Bring refund in from refunds.py.
List the names the package offers to other code.

type-hint.title: Type hints
type-hint.short: Type hints such as -> str or dict[str, int] note what kind of value a name should hold. Python does not enforce them.
type-hint.body:
A type hint is a note in the code about what kind of [[value|value]] a name should hold. In a def line, limit: int says the [[parameter|parameter]] limit should be a whole number, and -> str after the brackets says the function returns text. A variable can carry a hint too, as in names: list[str] = [].

Common hints are these. Older code writes List and Dict, imported from the typing module.

  • list[str] is a [[list|list]] of strings.
  • dict[str, Any] is a [[dict|dictionary]] with text keys and values of any type.
  • Optional[str], also written str | None, is a string or [[none|None]].
  • tuple[dict, list[str]] is a pair of a dictionary and a list.

Python does not check hints while the program runs. If you pass text where the hint says int, nothing stops you at that line. Hints are for human readers, editors and checking tools such as mypy, which can warn before the program runs. Data from outside, such as a web request, may not match its hint, so code still checks it with isinstance.

notes: data can be anything. The function promises to return a pair, a dictionary and a list of strings.

constant.title: Constant
constant.short: A constant is a module-level name in CAPITALS whose value should never change, such as MAX_RETRIES = 3.
constant.body:
Some values are settings that should never change while the program runs. Programmers give them a name in capital letters, at the top of the file, and call them constants. MAX_RETRIES = 3 is one.

Python does not lock a constant. Code could still assign a new value. The capitals are a convention that means "do not change this". A leading underscore, as in _MAX_RETRIES, adds "for use inside this file only" (see [[private-name|leading underscore]]).

A named constant beats a bare number, often called a magic number. The name and a comment above it say what the number means and why it has that value, and changing the value means changing one line. When a pull request replaces a repeated 80 with MAX_LINE_CHARS, it makes later changes safer.

A constant that nothing uses is a warning sign. A comment can promise a limit that no code enforces, so in review, search for the lines that read the constant.

example.title: Limits, named once
example.code:
MAX_WORKERS = 8
TIMEOUT_S = 30
MAX_LINE_CHARS = 80

if len(line) <= MAX_LINE_CHARS:
    shown = line
notes: At most 8 jobs run at once.
Each job gets 30 seconds.

Code reads the constant by name, so the reader sees what 80 means.
A line this short is shown whole.

decorator.title: Decorator
decorator.short: A decorator is a line starting with @ above a def or class. It wraps or marks what follows, as in @dataclass or @pytest.fixture.
decorator.body:
A decorator is a line that starts with @, placed right above a def or a class. It takes the [[function|function]] or class defined below, changes or labels it, and puts the result back under the same name. You write it once, and it applies to the whole definition.

Think of gift wrap. The present inside is the same, but the wrapping changes how it is handled.

Common decorators:

  • @dataclass above a class writes its setup code (see [[dataclass|dataclass]]).
  • @staticmethod above a method marks one that does not need its object (see [[staticmethod|staticmethod]]).
  • @pytest.fixture turns a function into a [[fixture|fixture]], a helper that tests ask for by name.
  • @pytest.mark.parametrize(...) runs the [[test|test]] below once for each input in a list.
  • @app.route('/orders') in web frameworks such as Flask connects a function to a web address.

A decorator can change behavior a lot while adding only one line to a [[diff|diff]], so it deserves a careful look in review.

object.title: Object
object.short: An object is a value that bundles data with the actions that work on it. In Python, every value is an object.
object.body:
An object is a [[value|value]] that bundles data with actions. The data are its [[attribute|attributes]], named values reached with a dot, such as cart.owner. The actions are its [[method|methods]], functions reached the same way, such as cart.add('lamp', 25).

Think of a car. It has data, such as its colour and fuel level, and actions, such as start and brake. You can press the brake pedal without knowing how the brakes work inside.

In Python every value is an object, even simple ones. The text 'hello' is an object with methods such as .upper() and .strip(). A list is an object with .append(). That is why the dot shows up everywhere in Python code.

A [[class|class]] defines each kind of object. Larger programs are built from objects that each own one part of the work, such as a database connection, a web request or a shopping cart.

class.title: Class
class.short: A class is a blueprint for objects. It lists the data each object holds and the methods it has.
class.body:
A class is a blueprint for [[object|objects]]. It describes what data each object of that kind holds and which [[method|methods]] it has. The keyword class starts it, followed by the name and a colon, and the indented block below holds the methods.

A cookie cutter is the usual picture. The cutter is the class. Each cookie you stamp out is an object made from it, called an [[instance|instance]]. All the cookies have the same shape, but each can have its own icing.

Class names use CapitalWords by convention, so OrderStore is a class while order_store is a variable or a module. Making an object from a class looks like calling a function, as in Cart('ana').

Tests often add small classes of their own, stand-ins that answer like a real part with canned data (see [[fake|fakes]]).

instance.title: Instance
instance.short: An instance is one object made from a class. Each instance has its own data, and all instances share the class's methods.
instance.body:
An instance is one [[object|object]] made from a [[class|class]]. cart = Cart('ana') makes a new instance of Cart and names it cart. Run that line twice and you get two separate instances. Changing one does not change the other.

Every instance has its own data, but all instances of a class share the same methods. Two cookies from one cutter have the same shape and separate icing.

How many instances exist, and who shares them, is a design decision with real effects. A web server often makes one instance of a service when it starts, and every request uses that one object, even when two requests run at the same time (see [[concurrency|concurrency]]).

So data that belongs to one request cannot live on that shared object. Code makes a fresh instance for each request instead, and drops it when the request ends (see [[shared-state|shared state]]).

attribute.title: Attribute
attribute.short: An attribute is a named value stored on an object, reached with a dot, as in cart.owner or self.timeout.
attribute.body:
An attribute is a named [[value|value]] that belongs to an [[object|object]]. You reach it with a dot, as in cart.owner or self.timeout. Read cart.owner as "the owner of cart".

You set an attribute with =, the same way as a [[variable|variable]]. cart.coupon = 'SPRING' changes the coupon on that one cart. If the attribute did not exist yet, Python creates it.

Attributes are how an object remembers things between [[method|method]] calls. A client object can read its settings into self.timeout and self.retries once, in its setup method, and use them on every request.

Asking for an attribute that does not exist stops the program with an AttributeError. This often happens when a new attribute is set only in the setup method and some code, such as an old [[test|test]], builds the object another way. A default on the class fixes that (see [[class-attribute|class attribute]]).

example.title: Setting and reading attributes
example.code:
self.retries = config.get('retries', 3)
self.timeout = float(config.get('timeout') or 30)
for attempt in range(self.retries):
    user = request.user
notes: Store an attribute on the client object. It comes from the settings, or 3 if none is set.
Another attribute, the timeout in seconds.

method.title: Method
method.short: A method is a function that belongs to a class. You call it on an object with a dot, as in cart.add(item).
method.body:
A method is a [[function|function]] defined inside a [[class|class]]. Every object made from the class has it. You call it through an object with a dot, as in cart.add('lamp', 25) or file.close().

A method works on the object it was called on. cart.add(...) adds to that cart and to no other cart. Inside the method, the object is available as [[self|self]].

Built-in values have methods too. 'abc'.upper() is a method of strings, items.append(x) is a method of lists, and data.get('id') is a method of dictionaries.

Splitting a class's work into methods keeps each one short. A pull request often moves a few lines out of a long method into a new one, because a second place in the code needs the same lines. That kind of move should not change what the code does, and a review can check that it does not.

self.title: self
self.short: self is the name a method uses for the object it was called on, so it can reach that object's data and other methods.
self.body:
When you call a [[method|method]] as cart.add('lamp', 25), Python passes the object, cart, in as an extra first argument. By convention the method names that first parameter self. So def add(self, name, price): receives three things, the object and two values.

Inside the method, self is how the code reaches the object's own [[attribute|attributes]] and methods. self.items reads this cart's items. self.total() calls another method on the same object.

Think of a form with "this applicant" printed on it. Each person who fills it in is "this applicant" on their own copy.

Anything stored on self lives as long as the object. If one object serves many callers, every caller sees and changes the same self data. That is the [[shared-state|shared state]] problem, and it is worth checking whenever a change adds a new self.something = ... line.

init.title: __init__ (constructor)
init.short: __init__ is the method Python runs automatically when it makes a new object. It gives the object its starting attributes.
init.body:
When you make a new object, as in Cart('ana'), Python creates an empty object of that class and then runs its __init__ method. __init__, said "dunder init" for the double underscores, is the constructor. Its job is to give the new object its starting [[attribute|attributes]].

The arguments in the creating call go to __init__, after [[self|self]]. In def __init__(self, owner):, owner receives the value passed in.

A child class's __init__ usually starts with super().__init__(...), which runs the parent's setup first (see [[override|super()]]).

Some code builds objects without running __init__, for example tests that call Cart.__new__(Cart) to skip slow setup. Any attribute set only in __init__ is then missing, and the first line that reads it fails.

example.code:
class Cache:

        self._prefix = f'{prefix}/'
        self._keys = set()
        self._closed = False
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.short: Inheritance lets a class build on another. class Child(Parent) gets all the parent's methods and adds or changes some.
inheritance.body:
A [[class|class]] can be based on another class. You write the parent in brackets, as in class EmailNotifier(Notifier):. This is inheritance. The new class, the child or subclass, gets every method and class attribute of the parent, the base class, without copying them. It then adds its own or [[override|replaces]] some.

Think of a standard job description that each branch office extends with local duties. The shared duties are written once.

A base class often holds the steps every child needs, such as logging and error handling, and leaves one method for each child to write. Each child fills in that one method its own way.

Inheritance also builds families of errors. class PaymentError(ValueError) is a new kind of error that code already catching ValueError still catches (see [[custom-exception|custom exception class]]). In review, a change to a base class affects every child, so look for all of them.

override.title: Overriding and super()
override.short: Overriding means a child class defines a method with the same name as its parent's. super() calls the parent's version from inside it.
override.body:
When a child class defines a [[method|method]] with the same name as one in its parent, the child's version wins for the child's objects. This is overriding. Python looks for a method on the object's own class first, and only then on the parent (see [[inheritance|inheritance]]).

Often the child wants the parent's work plus something extra. super() gives access to the parent's version. super().__init__(config) inside a child's __init__ runs the parent's setup first. The child then adds its own settings.

A child can skip super() on purpose. A test class can override the one method that would send a real network request, record the call and return fixed text, while every other method still runs for real.

A base class can also mark a method as abstract. Its version only raises NotImplementedError, and every child must override it. A review should check that an override keeps the parent's promises, such as what it returns and which errors it raises.

class-attribute.title: Class attribute
class-attribute.short: A class attribute is a value stored on the class itself and shared by all its instances, such as KIND = 'email'.
class-attribute.body:
Code sets most [[attribute|attributes]] on one object, usually in __init__ with self.name = .... You write a class attribute directly in the class body, outside any method. It belongs to the class, and every instance shares it.

When code reads obj.name, Python looks on the object first. If the object has no attribute of that name, it looks on the class. So a class attribute works as a default for every instance. One instance can still set its own value, which hides the class's value for that instance only.

A child class can replace a parent's class attribute with its own value (see [[inheritance|inheritance]]). A class-level default also protects code that builds an object without running __init__, such as an old test.

Class attributes suit fixed values, such as numbers and strings. A list or dictionary as a class attribute is one shared object. If any instance adds to it, every instance sees the change, which leads to the problems in [[shared-state|shared state]].

    check_command: str = ''

    def __init__(self, config):

bare = Notifier.__new__(Notifier)

private-name.title: Leading underscore
private-name.short: A name starting with one underscore, like _render, means "internal, not for use from outside". It is a convention, not a lock.
private-name.body:
Python has no way to truly hide a name. Instead, programmers follow a convention. A name that starts with one underscore, such as _render, _MAX_WORKERS or self._lock, means the name is internal to its file or class, and outside code should leave it alone.

Python does not enforce it. Other code can still read _MAX_WORKERS or call _render. The underscore works like a "staff only" sign on a door, not a lock. It tells readers which names are the public entry points and which are details that may change without warning.

This helps in review. A change to an underscore name affects only its own file, so the search for callers is short. A change to a public name may break code elsewhere, even in other projects.

[[test|Tests]] are the usual exception. They reach into internals to check them directly. Names with two underscores on each side, like __init__, are a different thing. They are special names that Python itself calls.

dataclass.title: dataclass
dataclass.short: @dataclass writes a class's __init__ for you from a list of typed fields. A frozen dataclass cannot be changed.
dataclass.body:
Many classes exist mainly to hold a few named values. Writing their __init__ by hand is repetitive. The @dataclass [[decorator|decorator]] does it for you. You list the fields with [[type-hint|type hints]], and Python writes an __init__ that accepts them, plus a readable printout and an equality check.

A field can have a default. For a [[list|list]] or [[dict|dictionary]] default you write field(default_factory=dict), which makes a fresh empty dictionary for every new object. A plain = {} would give every object the same dictionary, so Python refuses it.

@dataclass(frozen=True) makes objects that cannot be changed after creation. To get a version with one field different, you call dataclasses.replace, which builds a new object and leaves the original as it was. Frozen objects are safe to share, because nobody can change them under you (see [[shared-state|shared state]]).

staticmethod.title: staticmethod
staticmethod.short: @staticmethod marks a method that does not use self. It belongs to the class for tidiness but needs no object data.
staticmethod.body:
A normal [[method|method]] receives the object as [[self|self]]. Some functions belong with a class because they are part of its work, yet never touch the object's data. The @staticmethod [[decorator|decorator]] tells Python not to pass self to such a method. It then takes only its own parameters.

You can still call it through an object, as in self.error_entry(...), or through the class, as in Job.error_entry(...). Either way it behaves like a plain function stored inside the class. The marker also tells a reader that the result depends only on the inputs, never on the object's state.

A close cousin is @classmethod, which receives the class instead of the object. It is often used for extra ways to build an object, such as Order.from_json(text).

shared-state.title: Shared state
shared-state.short: Shared state is data stored where several users can change it. If two requests share one object, one can overwrite the other's data.
shared-state.body:
State is what a program remembers between steps. It becomes shared state when several users can read and change the same copy, for example an [[attribute|attribute]] on one object that many callers use.

Picture two cooks tracking two different orders on one notepad. If one cook tears off the page to start a new order while the other is halfway through, the second cook's notes are gone.

Servers hit this often. A server makes one service object at startup, and requests use it at the [[concurrency|same time]]. If the service starts each request with self.seen = {}, request B wipes request A's table while A is still using it.

The fix is to move everything a request remembers into objects the request creates for itself, and pass them along as arguments. The shared object keeps only settings that never change. When [[thread|threads]] truly must share data, a [[lock|lock]] lets one in at a time (see [[race-condition|race condition]]). In review, any attribute that a request writes on a long-lived object deserves a question.

exception.title: Exception
exception.short: A signal that something went wrong. It travels up through the functions that called the code until something catches it.
exception.body:
An exception is Python's way of saying "I cannot go on." When a line of code hits a problem it cannot handle, Python stops running that line and creates an exception [[object|object]]. The object records what kind of problem it was and carries a message about it.

Then the exception travels up. If the problem happened inside a [[function|function]], Python leaves that function and goes back to the line that [[call|called]] it. If nothing there handles the exception, Python leaves that function too, and so on up the chain. Picture a fire alarm that rings on one floor, then the floor above, until someone answers it. If nobody answers, the program stops and prints a [[error-message|traceback]].

Programmers like this design because the code that notices a problem is often not the code that knows what to do about it. A low-level function only has to say "this went wrong." A higher-level function decides whether to retry, report the problem, or give up. The code that answers the alarm uses [[try-except|try and except]]. Other languages call the same thing an error and catch it with try and catch.

try-except.title: try and except
try-except.short: A way to catch an exception and handle it, so one failed step does not crash the whole program.
try-except.body:
try and except let a program answer the alarm that an [[exception|exception]] raises. You put the risky lines under try:. Under except you write what to do if one of them fails. If nothing fails, Python skips the except block. If something fails, Python jumps straight to the except block and runs it instead of crashing.

You can say which exceptions to catch. except ValueError: catches only that kind. except Exception as exc: catches almost any error and puts it in the [[variable|variable]] exc, so the code can read its message. Python checks the except lines from top to bottom and uses the first one that matches.

A good except block turns the failure into something useful, such as an error entry with the cause, so one broken step does not end the whole job. A bad one catches everything and hides it. In review, look at what an except block does with the error. If it neither logs it nor passes it on, the problem disappears without a trace.

raise.title: raise
raise.short: The statement that creates an exception and throws it. It stops the current function and sends the problem up to its callers.
raise.body:
Python raises some [[exception|exceptions]] by itself, like AttributeError. Your own code can raise one too, with the raise statement. You write raise, then the exception, usually with a message, as in raise ValueError('price must be positive'). Python stops the current [[function|function]] at that line, and the exception starts travelling up.

Programmers raise an exception when a function finds a problem it should not hide. Returning an empty value would let the caller carry on as if all was fine. Raising forces someone to deal with the problem, and the message tells them what happened.

A good message names the cause and the fix. "config file not found at /etc/shop.json; set SHOP_CONFIG to its path" saves the reader a search. "error" does not.

A bare raise, with nothing after it, inside an except block throws the same exception again. Code does this to log a failure and still let a caller higher up handle it.

finally.title: finally
finally.short: A block after try that always runs, whether the code worked, failed or returned early. Programmers use it for cleanup.
finally.body:
A finally block sits after try, and after any except blocks. Python runs it no matter how the try block ends. It runs if the code finished normally. It runs if an [[exception|exception]] flew out. It even runs if the code hit a [[return|return]] statement. Think of switching off the lights when you leave a room, however you leave it.

Programmers put cleanup there, the work that must happen even when things go wrong. Closing a file, releasing a [[lock|lock]], shutting down a [[thread-pool|thread pool]] and putting a setting back are common examples.

Python's with statement is a shorter way to get the same guarantee for one object. with open(path) as f: closes the file at the end of the block, whatever happens inside. In review, look for cleanup that sits after the main work with no finally. One error skips it.

custom-exception.title: Custom exception class
custom-exception.short: Your own named kind of exception, made by inheriting from a built-in one, so callers can catch exactly that problem.
custom-exception.body:
Python has many built-in [[exception|exception]] types, such as ValueError and TypeError. You can make your own with a [[class|class]] that inherits from one of them. The class often holds nothing but a [[comment|docstring]], because all its behavior comes from the parent. What matters is the name.

A named exception lets callers react to one specific problem. An except EmptyReplyError: line catches only that problem and lets every other error pass by. Because of [[inheritance|inheritance]], the new exception is still a ValueError. Older code that catches ValueError keeps working with no change.

Order matters when you catch them. Python uses the first except line that matches. A specific error is also an instance of its parent type, so the specific except line must come first. With the order reversed, the general line catches the specific error and handles it the wrong way.

algorithm.title: Algorithm
algorithm.short: A step-by-step method for solving a problem, written precisely enough for a computer to follow.
algorithm.body:
An algorithm is a fixed list of steps that turns an input into an output. A recipe is an algorithm for a cake. Long division is an algorithm for dividing numbers. In a [[program|program]], an algorithm is usually one or a few [[function|functions]] that carry out the steps.

Programmers think in algorithms because the steps decide what the program does in every case, not only the common one. Two algorithms can give the same answer on easy inputs and very different answers on hard ones. So a programmer asks what happens with an empty input, a huge input, or a strange one.

Speed is the other question. Finding repeats by checking every pair in a list of 1,000 items takes about 500,000 comparisons. Putting the items in a [[set|set]] takes about 1,000 steps. A change that looks small can turn a fast step into a slow one when the input grows.

When you review a change to an algorithm, run one ordinary input and one edge case through the steps by hand.
