budget.title: Budgets and truncation
budget.short: A fixed allowance, such as 4,000 characters, that code shares out between parts of a text, cutting each part to fit.
budget.body:
A budget in code works like a money budget. There is a fixed amount to spend, and the code decides who gets how much. The currency is often characters or bytes, for example in a log line, a database field, an error report or a message sent to another service.

Truncation means cutting text to fit. The simplest cut keeps the first N characters. That works for a short name. For a long file or log it can hide what matters, because the last lines, such as the final ValueError: ... of an error log, are often the important ones. A head and tail cut keeps the start and the end and drops the middle, with a note that says how much was dropped.

Sharing is the other half. If one message holds two long fields and one short one, giving each long field budget // 2 (see [[number|integer division]]) leaves room for the short field. Without a split, the first long field can use it all and push the short field, perhaps an exit code, out.

In review, ask what the reader of the cut text needs to see, and check that the code keeps it.

notes: Defines a function that fits one piece of text into its budget.

hash.title: Hashing and fingerprints
hash.short: A short fixed-size code computed from data. Equal data gives an equal code, so programs use it to spot repeats.
hash.body:
A hash function reads any amount of data and produces a short code of fixed size, called a hash or fingerprint. SHA-256, a common one, always gives 64 hexadecimal characters, the digits 0 to 9 and the letters a to f. Equal input always gives an equal fingerprint. Change one character of the input and the fingerprint changes completely. Two different inputs with the same SHA-256 fingerprint are so unlikely that programs treat it as impossible.

That makes a fingerprint a cheap way to ask "have I seen this exact data before?" Comparing two 64-character codes is fast, even when the data behind them is a 100 KB file. git names every [[commit|commit]] by a hash of its contents.

To fingerprint structured data, first turn it into text in a fixed form. {'a': 1, 'b': 2} and {'b': 2, 'a': 1} hold the same data, but they print in a different order. json.dumps(data, sort_keys=True) gives both the same text, so they get the same fingerprint.

Python's [[dict|dictionaries]] use a faster, simpler kind of hash to find keys (see [[hash-table|hash table]]).

example.title: Fingerprinting a small record
example.code:
import hashlib
import json

record = {'path': 'docs/intro.md', 'version': 1}
text = json.dumps(record, sort_keys=True)
fingerprint = hashlib.sha256(text.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()
print(len(fingerprint))
notes: Loads Python's module of hash functions.
Loads the JSON module, which turns data into text.
A small record, a dictionary with two fields.
Turns it into JSON text with the keys in sorted order, so equal data always gives equal text.
Turns the text into bytes, hashes them with SHA-256, and writes the hash as hexadecimal text.
Prints 64. Every SHA-256 fingerprint has that length, whatever the size of the input.

hash-table.title: Hash table (how a dict finds keys fast)
hash-table.short: The structure behind a Python dictionary. It uses a hash of the key to jump straight to the right slot instead of searching.
hash-table.body:
A Python [[dict|dictionary]] finds a key almost at once, whether it holds 10 entries or 10 million. It can because it is a hash table. When you store a key, Python computes a [[hash|hash]] of the key and uses that number to pick a slot in a hidden array. To look the key up later, Python computes the same hash and goes straight to the same slot.

Think of a cloakroom. You hand over your coat and get ticket 47. Later the attendant goes straight to hook 47 instead of checking every coat. The hash is the ticket number, worked out from the key itself.

A [[set|set]] works the same way, without the values. That is why "is this in the set?" stays fast while "is this in the list?" gets slower as the list grows.

The method setdefault asks "seen it before?" in one step. seen.setdefault(key, value) stores value if the key is new and returns it. If the key is already there, it changes nothing and returns the value stored first. A separate check followed by a store takes two steps, and two [[thread|threads]] can both slip in between them (see [[race-condition|race condition]]).

example.code:
seen = {}
first = seen.setdefault('3f9a...e1', 'item-0')
print(first)
again = seen.setdefault('3f9a...e1', 'item-5')
print(again)
print(seen)
notes: An empty table.
'3f9a...e1' stands for a 64-character fingerprint. It is new, so setdefault stores 'item-0' and returns it.
Prints item-0, the value just stored. This item is new.

recursion.title: Recursion
recursion.short: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece, with a stopping rule so it ends.
recursion.body:
Recursion means a [[function|function]] calls itself. It fits data that has the same shape inside itself, like a [[dict|dictionary]] whose values are more dictionaries, or a folder that holds more folders. The function handles one level, and for each value one level down it [[call|calls]] itself again.

Every recursive function needs a stopping rule, called the base case. Without one, it calls itself forever, and Python stops it after about 1,000 nested calls with a RecursionError. Russian nesting dolls are the usual picture. You open a doll, find a smaller one inside, and open that, until you reach the solid doll in the middle.

Plain values, such as numbers and short text, are natural base cases. A depth limit adds a second one for safety. Data can contain itself, as after d['self'] = d, and then only a depth limit stops the function. In review, find the base cases first and check that every path reaches one.

regex.title: Regular expression
regex.short: A small pattern language for finding text, such as every order number in a log or every {{name}} tag in a template.
regex.body:
A regular expression, or regex, is a pattern that describes text. Python's re [[module-import|module]] can search a [[string|string]] for any text that matches the pattern. Most characters match themselves. A few have special meanings.

  • . matches any one character, and \. matches a real dot.
  • \d matches a digit, and \w matches a letter, a digit or an underscore.
  • + means "one or more of the thing before it", * means "zero or more", and ? means "optional".
  • ( ) captures the matched part, so the code can read it afterwards.
  • (?: ) groups a part without capturing it.

Programmers reach for regex when "does this text contain X?" is not enough and they need structure out of the text. Regex is compact but hard to read, so careful code puts a comment or an example next to each pattern. In review, test a changed pattern against one text it should match and one it should not.

example.title: Reading the parts of a template tag
example.code:
import re

TAG = re.compile(r'\{\{(\w+)(?::(\w+))?\}\}')
m = TAG.search('Hello {{name:upper}}, your order shipped.')
print(m.group(1))
print(m.group(2))
print(TAG.findall('{{a}} and {{b:lower}}'))
notes: Loads Python's regex module.
The pattern. Two opening braces, a name, an optional colon and format, then two closing braces.
Searches a template. m holds the first match.
Prints name, the first captured part.
Prints upper, the optional format.

parsing.title: Parsing
parsing.short: Turning text into structured data a program can use, like turning a JSON reply into a Python dictionary.
parsing.body:
Parsing means reading text and building structured data from it. A web service replies with text, and the program needs a [[dict|dictionary]] with fields it can read. json.loads parses [[json|JSON]] text into that dictionary. It is strict. If the text is not exactly JSON, it raises json.JSONDecodeError.

Text from outside is not always exact. A reply may carry a remark after the JSON, or a sentence before it. A parser can be strict and refuse such input, or lenient and dig the data out.

Lenient parsing needs care. Reading one complete JSON value from the start and ignoring a remark after it is safe, because the data is clearly there. Grabbing the first {...} found anywhere in a paragraph is risky, because the paragraph may contain an example object. Running on the wrong data is worse than failing with a clear error. In review, ask what the new parser accepts that the old one refused, and whether any of it could be the wrong data.

deep-copy.title: Copy and deep copy
deep-copy.short: Making a fully separate duplicate of an object, so that changing the copy cannot change the original.
deep-copy.body:
In Python, b = a does not copy anything. It gives the same [[object|object]] a second name. Change the object through b and a sees the change, because there is only one object. It is like two people holding keys to the same locker.

A shallow copy makes a new outer object, but the objects inside it are still shared. dict(order) and list(items) are shallow copies. A deep copy duplicates everything, all the way down, so nothing is shared. Python's copy.deepcopy(x) makes one.

Code deep-copies data it is about to edit when the original must stay as it was, for example a request that the next step will use again. The reverse also matters. A deep copy carries everything the original already held. If code copies an object and then adds something the original already had, the copy now holds it twice.

example.title: A second name versus a real copy
example.code:
import copy

request = {'questions': ['Where is my order?'], 'goals': []}
same = request
r = copy.deepcopy(request)
r['goals'].append(r['questions'][0])
r['questions'] = []
print(request['questions'])
print(same is request)
notes: Loads Python's copy module.
A request with one question and no goals.
A second name for the same object. Nothing is copied.

thread.title: Thread
thread.short: One line of work inside a running program. A program can run several threads at the same time.
thread.body:
A [[program|program]] normally does one thing at a time, line after line. A thread is one such line of work. A program can start more threads, and they run at the same time. Picture a kitchen with several cooks. Each cook follows a recipe, and all of them share the same kitchen.

Threads help most when the work spends its time waiting. A request to a web service mostly waits for the reply. While one thread waits, others can make their own requests. Five downloads on five threads can finish in about the time of the slowest one.

Threads share the program's memory. That is useful, because they can all write results into one [[list|list]]. It is also a source of bugs, because two threads can touch the same data at once. The lessons on [[race-condition|race conditions]] and [[lock|locks]] cover that.

One limit shapes a lot of code. Python cannot stop a thread from outside. If a call hangs forever, the thread running it hangs too. The program can only stop waiting for it, as the [[timeout|timeout]] lesson shows.

example.title: Running one job on its own thread, with a limit on the wait
example.code:
thread = threading.Thread(target=download)
thread.start()
thread.join(timeout=10)
finished = not thread.is_alive()
if not finished:
    print('still downloading, moving on')
notes: Creates a thread whose job is download, a function defined elsewhere. It has not started yet.
Starts the thread. From here on it runs at the same time as the rest of the program.
Waits for the thread to finish, but stops waiting after 10 seconds.
True if the download ended in time.
The thread is still running.
The program cannot stop the thread. It can only stop waiting and carry on.

thread-pool.title: Thread pool and futures
thread-pool.short: A fixed team of worker threads that takes jobs from a queue. A Future is the ticket for a job's result.
thread-pool.body:
Starting a new [[thread|thread]] for every small job is wasteful, and a thousand threads at once can overload a machine. A thread pool keeps a fixed team of worker threads instead. You hand it jobs. Each free worker takes the next job from a queue, and when it finishes, it takes another.

When you hand over a job with pool.submit(...), you get back a Future at once. A Future is like the buzzer a restaurant gives you when you order. The food is not ready yet, but the buzzer tells you when it is. future.result() gives you the job's [[return|return]] value once it is done. wait(...) waits for several Futures and can stop as soon as the first one finishes.

Python's ThreadPoolExecutor is a thread pool. Jobs finish in any order, so code that needs results in the original order keeps a [[dict|dictionary]] from each Future to its position.

Watch how the pool ends. Leaving a with ThreadPoolExecutor(...) block waits for every job, including a stuck one. pool.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True) cancels queued jobs and does not wait for running ones.

concurrency.title: Concurrency
concurrency.short: Having two or more pieces of work in progress at the same time, such as two requests handled by one server.
concurrency.body:
Concurrency means more than one piece of work is in progress at once. The pieces may truly run at the same moment on different processor cores, or they may take turns quickly. Either way, the second one starts before the first one ends. [[thread|Threads]] are one way to get concurrency in Python, and async code is another.

Concurrency is good for speed and bad for simple reasoning. Code that is correct when it runs alone can break when another copy runs beside it. Any data that both pieces of work can see becomes a place where they can collide.

Concurrency often hides at two levels. Inside one request, code may run several jobs at once on a [[thread-pool|thread pool]]. Across requests, a server may handle two users at the same time with one shared [[object|object]]. The second level is easy to miss, because each request's code looks like it runs alone. That is where [[shared-state|shared state]] bugs come from.

In review, take each piece of data the change writes and ask who else can see it at the same time.

example.title: Two requests in progress at once
example.code:
service = OrderService()
a = threading.Thread(target=service.handle, args=(request_a,))
b = threading.Thread(target=service.handle, args=(request_b,))
a.start()
b.start()
a.join()
b.join()
notes: One object, shared by every request the server handles.
Prepares a thread for the first request.

The second request starts before the first one ends. Both now run methods on the same service.

race-condition.title: Race condition
race-condition.short: A bug where the result depends on which thread gets somewhere first, so it shows up only some of the time.
race-condition.body:
A race condition is a bug whose outcome depends on timing. Two [[thread|threads]] touch the same data, and the result changes with which one goes first. Most runs come out fine. Now and then the order is unlucky and the data ends up wrong. That makes race conditions hard to find, because they rarely show up when you look for them.

A classic shape is "check, then act". Thread A checks that a slot is empty. Before A writes, thread B checks the same slot, and it is still empty. Both write, and both believe they were first. Another shape is a reset. Request B replaces a shared table with an empty one while request A is still using it, and A's entries vanish.

The fixes are to do the check and the write in one step (see [[hash-table|setdefault]]), to guard the steps with a [[lock|lock]], or to stop sharing the data at all.

A good test for a race does not rely on luck or on sleeping. It uses events to pause one thread at a known point, runs the other, and then lets the first go on. That forces the unlucky order every time.

example.title: Check, then act, step by step
example.code:
if key not in cache:
    # thread B runs the same check here and also finds no key
    cache[key] = build(key)

value = cache.setdefault(key, candidate)
notes: Thread A checks. The key is not there.
Before A writes, the system switches to thread B, which passes the same check.
Both threads build the value and write it. One of them does the work for nothing, or overwrites the other.
One fix. setdefault checks and writes in one step, so only the first thread's value is kept.

lock.title: Lock
lock.short: A tool that lets only one thread at a time into a section of code, so steps that belong together are not interrupted.
lock.body:
A lock guards a piece of code. A [[thread|thread]] must take the lock before it enters, and it gives the lock back when it leaves. If another thread holds the lock, the newcomer waits. Think of the single bathroom key at a cafe. Whoever holds the key is inside, and everyone else waits for it.

Locks fix [[race-condition|race conditions]] by making a group of steps happen as one. In Python you create a lock with threading.Lock(). A block that starts with with self._lock: holds the lock. Python takes it at the start of the block and releases it at the end, even if an [[exception|exception]] is raised inside.

Hold a lock only around your own bookkeeping, never around a call that might hang. If code holds a lock while it writes to a slow service, and the write hangs, every other thread that needs the lock hangs too. A safer shape takes the lock to check and record, releases it for the slow call, then takes it again to see whether anything changed in the meantime.

Two threads that take two locks in opposite orders can wait on each other forever, which is called a deadlock.

example.title: Checking under a lock before and after a slow write
example.code:
def put(self, key, value):
    with self._lock:
        if self._closed:
            return False
        self._keys.add(key)
    self._store.put(self._prefix + key, value)
    with self._lock:
        closed = self._closed
    if closed:
        self._store.clear(self._prefix + key)
        return False
    return True
notes: Stores a value. self._lock was created in __init__ with threading.Lock().

timeout.title: Timeout and deadline
timeout.short: Giving up on something after a set time. A deadline is the same limit stated as a moment, such as start time plus 30 seconds.
timeout.body:
A timeout is a limit on waiting. If an answer has not come within the limit, the program stops waiting and treats the job as failed. A deadline is the same idea stated as a moment, "start time plus 30 seconds", instead of a length of time.

Programs need timeouts because the outside world can hang. A web service may never reply. Without a limit, the code that waits for it waits forever, and so does the user. Many libraries wait forever by default. Python's requests.get has no timeout unless you pass one.

The details matter.

  • Start each job's clock when the job really starts. A job queued behind busy workers should not lose its time while it waits.
  • Measure with time.monotonic(). A wall clock can jump when the computer corrects its time. A monotonic clock only moves forward.
  • Decide what happens to the late result. A job that timed out may still finish later on its [[thread|thread]], and nothing should use its result by mistake.

A comment or setting that promises a timeout proves nothing. In review, find the line that enforces it.

contextvar.title: Context variable
contextvar.short: A variable whose value belongs to the current task, so code running at the same time each sees its own value.
contextvar.body:
The whole program shares a normal module-level [[variable|variable]]. If one [[thread|thread]] sets it, another thread that reads it a moment later sees that value. That breaks when two requests run at the same time and each needs its own value, such as its request id for the logs.

A context variable, from Python's contextvars module, solves this. Each thread or async task has its own context, a private set of values for every context variable. VAR.set(value) changes the value in the current context only and returns a token, which works as a receipt. VAR.reset(token) puts the old value back, and VAR.get() reads the current context's value.

Why not pass the value as a [[parameter|parameter]]? Because it must travel through many layers of code that do not know about it, such as a logging call deep inside a library.

Worker threads in a [[thread-pool|thread pool]] do not inherit the context. Code that hands a job to a pool wraps it in contextvars.copy_context().run so the job sees the caller's values.

example.title: Setting a per-request value and putting it back
example.code:
REQUEST_ID = contextvars.ContextVar('request_id', default=None)

def log_saved():
    log.info('saved order request_id=%s', REQUEST_ID.get())

token = REQUEST_ID.set('req-42')
try:
    handle(request)
finally:
    REQUEST_ID.reset(token)
notes: Creates the context variable once, at module level. Its value starts as None.
A logging helper deep inside the code.
Reads the request id for the current context only. No parameter carried it here.
At the start of a request, sets this request's id and keeps the receipt.

Does the work. Somewhere inside, log_saved runs and sees req-42.

Puts the previous value back.

api.title: API and HTTP request
api.short: An agreed way for one program to ask another for something, often by sending an HTTP request over the network.
api.body:
An API, short for application programming interface, is a set of requests that one [[program|program]] accepts from others, with fixed names and data shapes. A restaurant menu is a fair picture. You can order what is on it, in the way it says, and the kitchen stays out of sight.

Many APIs work over HTTP, the same system a web browser uses. The calling program sends a request to an address such as https://api.example.com/orders/42. The request has a method, such as GET to read or POST to send data. It has headers, extra details such as the key that proves who is asking. It may also have a body, often [[json|JSON]]. The server sends back a response with a status code and a body. 200 means success, 404 means "not found", 429 means "too many requests, slow down", and codes from 500 up mean the server failed.

Network requests fail in ordinary ways. Good client code sets a [[timeout|timeout]], retries errors that may pass, such as 429 and 503, waits longer before each new try, and fails at once on errors that waiting cannot fix, such as a bad key.

example.title: One API request made by hand
example.code:
import requests

response = requests.get(
    'https://api.example.com/orders/42',
    headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {api_key}'},
    timeout=10,
)
print(response.status_code)
print(response.json()['status'])
notes: Loads requests, a popular Python library for HTTP.
Sends an HTTP GET request and waits for the response.

A header. The key proves who is asking.
Gives up after 10 seconds instead of waiting forever.

test.title: Test
test.short: Code that runs your code with a known input and checks that the result is what you expect.
test.body:
A test is a small [[program|program]] that checks another program. It sets up an input, runs the code under test, and compares the result with the expected one. If they match, the test passes. If not, it fails and says where.

People also test by hand, by running the program and looking at it. Tests in code are exact, because they compare values instead of impressions. They are repeatable, so the same checks run again after every change, in seconds. And they record intent. A test named test_exit_code_survives_long_output tells the next programmer what the code must do.

In Python a test is usually a [[function|function]] whose name starts with test_. It uses [[assert|assert]] lines for its checks, and a tool such as [[pytest|pytest]] finds it and runs it.

A test for a bug fix should fail on the old code and pass on the new code. If it passes on both, it does not prove the fix. In review, ask whether the author ran it against the old code.

example.title: A small test
notes: A test function. pytest runs it because its name starts with test_.
The input, a command result with two 10,000-character outputs and an exit code.
Runs the code under test.
Check one. The field after the long outputs is still shown.
Check two. stderr got a real share of the budget, at least 1,000 characters.

assert.title: assert
assert.short: A line that states something must be true. If it is false, the test stops and fails right there.
assert.body:
assert is a Python statement. It takes a condition, an expression that is [[boolean|True or False]]. If the condition is True, nothing happens and the next line runs. If it is False, Python raises AssertionError, and the [[test|test]] fails at that line.

When [[pytest|pytest]] runs the test, a failed assert reports more than "failed". pytest shows the line and the values on each side. If assert total == 45 fails, it prints what total really held. That turns a red mark into a clue.

Good asserts check what matters to the user, not how the code got there. A test of an error report should check that the report names the cause and keeps the data already gathered, not which internal lines ran.

An assert should also fail for the right reason. Run a new test on the old code and read the failure. If it fails because of a typo or a missing argument, it is not testing the bug.

example.title: Two asserts on two users of one store
example.code:
def test_two_requests_keep_their_own_values():
    store = FakeStore()
    a, b = Cache(store, 'req-a'), Cache(store, 'req-b')

    a.put('result', 'from a')
    b.put('result', 'from b')

    assert a.get('result') == 'from a'
    assert b.get('result') == 'from b'
notes: A test function.
One fake store, shared like a real one.
Two requests that use the same store, each through its own Cache.
Request a stores a value under the key result.
Request b stores a different value under the same key.
Must be True. Request a still reads its own value. Without the per-request prefix, b's write would have replaced it.
Must be True. Request b reads its own value.

pytest.title: pytest
pytest.short: The tool that finds test files and test functions, runs them, and reports which passed and which failed.
pytest.body:
pytest is the most common tool for running Python [[test|tests]]. You do not list your tests anywhere, because pytest finds them by name. It looks for files named test_*.py and, inside them, for functions whose names start with test_. It runs each one and prints a summary, such as "24 passed".

pytest adds several tools around the plain [[assert|assert]].

  • Detailed failure reports that show the values in a failed assert.
  • @pytest.mark.parametrize, a [[decorator|decorator]] that runs one test with many inputs.
  • Markers such as [[xfail|xfail]], for tests that are expected to fail.
  • [[fixture|Fixtures]], ready-made helpers a test asks for by name.
  • pytest.importorskip('numpy'), which skips a whole file when a module is missing instead of failing it.

pytest -k cart runs only the tests whose names contain "cart", and pytest -x stops at the first failure. A skipped test counts as neither passed nor failed, so in review, read the skip count too.

fake.title: Fake, stub and mock
fake.short: A stand-in for a slow or unpredictable part, such as a web service or a clock, so a test runs fast and the same every time.
fake.body:
Real web services are slow, may cost money, and can answer differently each time. Real databases and files carry state from one run to the next. A [[test|test]] that used them would be slow, expensive and unreliable. So tests replace those parts with stand-ins.

  • A fake is a working, simplified version, such as an in-memory [[dict|dictionary]] in place of a database.
  • A stub returns canned answers and does nothing else.
  • A mock also records how it was called, so the test can check the calls.

Good tests keep the code under test real and fake only the edges. A fake should answer in the same shape as the real part, including its errors, or the test proves less than it seems.

A fake can stand in for time, too. A test can give the code a clock that moves only when the test moves it. Then it can check a 10-second limit without waiting 10 seconds, and no result depends on how fast the machine is.

end-to-end.title: End-to-end test
end-to-end.short: A test that runs the whole flow, from request to answer, and checks what the user would actually get.
end-to-end.body:
A unit test checks one small piece, such as one [[function|function]], on its own. An end-to-end test runs the whole flow from start to finish, the way a user would, and checks the final outcome.

Both kinds are useful. Unit [[test|tests]] are fast and point straight at the broken piece. But pieces that each work can still fail together. A wrong order of steps, a value dropped between two functions, or a setting that never reaches the code that needs it are bugs that no unit test sees.

A middle kind, often called an integration test, runs several real pieces together and replaces only the slow or costly edges with [[fake|fakes]]. It catches many of the same bugs at a fraction of the cost.

End-to-end tests are slower and break for more reasons, so projects keep fewer of them. In review, ask which kind of test covers the change. A bug in the order of steps needs a test that runs the steps together.

example.title: Running the real flow with only the edge faked
example.code:
def test_checkout_sends_one_receipt():
    sent = []
    app = make_app(send_email=lambda to, text: sent.append((to, text)))

    response = app.checkout(cart=sample_cart(), user='ana@example.com')

    assert response.status == 'paid'
    assert len(sent) == 1

xfail.title: Expected failure (xfail)
xfail.short: A pytest marker for a test that is expected to fail, used to record a known bug. With strict=True, an unexpected pass fails the run.
xfail.body:
Sometimes you know a bug exists before you fix it. You can write the test that shows the bug now, but it would fail and turn the whole suite red. @pytest.mark.xfail tells [[pytest|pytest]] that a test is expected to fail. pytest still runs it. It reports a failure as "xfailed", and that does not count against the run.

What if the test passes? By default pytest only reports "xpassed". With strict=True, an unexpected pass makes the run fail. That forces a decision. If the bug is gone, someone must remove the marker on purpose. The pull request that fixes the bug then deletes the marker in its [[diff|diff]], and the same test must pass.

A marker hides a failure, so it can hide the wrong failure too. A test may fail because of a TypeError in its own setup and never reach the check for the bug. Running pytest with --runxfail ignores the markers and prints each real failure, so you can check that every test fails because of its own bug.

fixture.title: Fixture and monkeypatch
fixture.short: A ready-made helper that pytest hands to a test when the test names it as a parameter. monkeypatch is one of them.
fixture.body:
Many tests need the same setup, such as a temporary folder, a database, or a changed setting. A fixture is pytest's way to provide it. You write the fixture's name as a [[parameter|parameter]] of the test function. pytest sees the name, creates the fixture, and passes it in. After the test, pytest runs the fixture's cleanup. You define your own with the @pytest.fixture [[decorator|decorator]], often in a shared file named conftest.py.

monkeypatch is a fixture built into pytest. It lets a test swap a value for the length of one test. monkeypatch.setattr(obj, 'name', new_value) replaces an [[attribute|attribute]] or a [[constant|constant]]. When the test ends, pytest puts the original back. Even if the test fails, the next test sees the real value.

A common use is shrinking a limit. A real timeout of 300 seconds would make a test far too slow, so the test sets it to 0.3 seconds. tmp_path, another built-in fixture, gives each test a fresh empty folder.

example.title: Shrinking a timeout for one test
example.code:
def test_stuck_job_times_out(monkeypatch, tmp_path):
    monkeypatch.setattr(jobs, 'TIMEOUT_S', 0.3)
    monkeypatch.setattr(jobs, 'MAX_WORKERS', 1)
    log_file = tmp_path / 'run.log'
    result = jobs.run_all([stuck_job, quick_job], log=log_file)
    assert 'TimeoutError' in result[0]['error']

regression.title: Regression
regression.short: Something that used to work and breaks after a change. Tests that keep passing are the guard against it.
regression.body:
A regression is a step backwards. A feature worked yesterday, someone changed the code today, and now the feature is broken. Often the change was meant to fix something else. Regressions are common because code is connected in ways that are easy to miss.

[[test|Tests]] are the main defense. Once a behavior has a test, any change that breaks it turns the test red before the change merges. A test written for this purpose is sometimes called a guard. It passes on the old code and must keep passing on the new code.

A good fix thinks about what it might undo. Say an earlier change tuned a list view to show many short rows, and a new change wants to show long text in full. The simplest version gives every row's text the full space, so fewer rows fit, and no test notices that the earlier tuning is gone. A careful author adds a guard test that counts the rows. It passes before and after the real fix, and fails on the simple version.

In review, ask what else depends on the changed code and whether a test covers it.

example.title: A guard test
example.code:
def test_row_text_is_still_cut_at_80():
    rows = [{'name': f'Document {i}', 'description': 'd' * 500} for i in range(5)]

    summary = summarize(rows, budget=4000)

    assert f'"{"d" * 80}..." (500 chars)' in summary
    assert summary.count('row[') == 5
notes: A guard test. It passes on the old code and on the new.

lint.title: Linter
lint.short: A tool that reads code without running it and flags style problems and simple mistakes. ruff and ESLint are linters.
lint.body:
A linter reads [[source-file|source files]] and reports problems without running the code. Some problems are real mistakes, such as a name used but never defined, or an import nobody uses. Others are about style, such as single versus double quotes, or a missing docstring. A team agrees on the rules once, and the linter applies them to everyone.

Python projects often use ruff, flake8 or pylint, and JavaScript projects use ESLint. A formatter, such as ruff format, Black or Prettier, goes one step further and rewrites the layout of the code itself. Settings usually live in a file such as pyproject.toml.

Linters run in two common places. A pre-commit hook runs them on the changed files before each [[commit|commit]], and [[ci|CI]] runs them on every pull request.

A linter has limits. Most do not flag a [[parameter|parameter]] that nothing reads anymore, or a comment that no longer matches the code. A person has to catch those. A clean lint run means the code follows the rules, not that it works.

$ ruff check --fix app/pricing.py
$ ruff format --check app

git.title: git
git.short: The tool that records versions of a project's files, so you can see every change, who made it, and go back.
git.body:
git is a version control system. It keeps the full history of a project's files in a hidden folder named .git, next to the files. Every saved version records which lines changed, who changed them, when, and why. You can compare any two versions, see who last touched a line, or bring back an old version. A folder that git tracks is called a repository, or repo.

Programmers rely on git because code changes all the time, often by several people at once. Without it, nobody could answer "what changed since this last worked?" With it, that question is one command.

The basic cycle is short. You edit [[source-file|files]]. git status lists what changed. git add picks the changes to save. git commit saves them as one [[commit|commit]] with a message. Commits form a history, and [[branch|branches]] let separate lines of work go on side by side. [[diff|Diffs]] show exactly what changed between two versions.

Sites such as GitHub and GitLab host git repositories and add [[pull-request|pull requests]] on top. git show branch:path prints a file as it is on another branch without switching to it, which helps when reviewing.

example.title: Looking at a project's history
example.code:
$ git status
$ git log --oneline -3

4b8a0d2 feat(cart): add coupons
1c3e5f9 test(cart): cover an empty cart
$ git blame -L 40,45 app/cart.py
$ git show main:app/cart.py

commit.title: Commit
commit.short: One saved change to the project, with a message that says what changed and why, and an id like 9f2c1e7.
commit.body:
A commit is a snapshot of the project at one moment, saved with a message. It records the changes since the commit before it, the author, the time, and a link to that parent commit. The chain of parents is the history. Each commit gets a unique id, a [[hash|hash]] of its contents, usually shown short, as in 9f2c1e7.

Good commits are small and have one purpose, so they are easy to review and easy to undo. The message has a short first line, the subject, then a blank line and a body that explains why. Many projects follow a pattern called Conventional Commits, type(scope): what changed. fix marks a bug fix, feat a new feature and test new tests, and the scope names the part of the code.

A good body says what was wrong, what changes, and what stays the same on purpose. It can also give evidence, such as a measurement before and after, and credit whoever found the problem.

branch.title: Branch
branch.short: A named line of commits, so work on one change stays separate until it is ready, like fix/cart-coupon.
branch.body:
A branch is a name that points at a [[commit|commit]]. When you commit on a branch, the name moves forward to the new commit. Each branch is its own line of work. You can switch between branches, and changes on one do not touch the others until you merge them.

A project has a main branch, often named main, that holds the shared, accepted code. Some projects use develop for this. Work happens on separate branches started from it. When the work is done and reviewed, a [[pull-request|pull request]] merges it back.

Branch names often follow a pattern that says what the branch is for, such as a type, a ticket number and a short description, as in fix/SHOP-142-cart-coupon or feat/order-export. When a branch falls behind main, the author either merges main into it or rebases it, which replays its commits on top of the newer main.

example.title: Starting a branch from main
example.code:
$ git switch main
$ git pull
$ git switch -c fix/cart-coupon
$ git add app/cart.py tests/test_cart.py
$ git commit
$ git push -u origin fix/cart-coupon

diff.title: Diff
diff.short: A listing of the lines removed (-) and added (+) between two versions of a file. It is how code changes are read.
diff.body:
A diff shows what changed between two versions. Lines that start with - were removed. Lines that start with + were added. Lines that start with a space did not change. They are context, there to show where the change sits.

Reading a diff starts with the headers.

  • --- a/path is the old file, and +++ b/path is the new one.
  • A line like @@ -40,5 +40,7 @@ def fill_template( opens a hunk, one block of nearby changes. -40,5 means that the block starts at line 40 of the old file and shows 5 of its lines. +40,7 means the same block is 7 lines long in the new file. The text after the second @@ names the function the change is in.

A changed line appears as a removal followed by an addition. To understand a diff, read the - lines as "before" and the + lines as "after", and ask what behavior differs. A diff shows only nearby lines, so open the whole file when the change depends on code further away.

example.title: A hunk that replaces a silent blank with a marker
example.code:
--- a/app/templates.py
+++ b/app/templates.py
@@ -40,5 +40,7 @@ def fill_template(
         value = store.get(key)
         if value is None:
-            return ''
+            # Say what is missing instead of leaving a silent gap.
+            log.debug('missing template key %r', key)
+            return f'[missing: {key}]'
         if fmt:
             value = apply_format(value, fmt)

pull-request.title: Pull request (PR)
pull-request.short: A request to merge a branch into the main branch. Others review the diff and automated checks run before it merges.
pull-request.body:
A pull request, or PR, is how a change gets into the shared code on sites such as GitHub. You push your [[branch|branch]] and open a PR that asks to merge it into a target branch, usually main. The PR page shows the [[diff|diff]], a title, and a description that explains the change. GitLab calls the same thing a merge request.

The PR is where the checking happens before the merge.

  • People [[code-review|review]] the diff and leave comments on specific lines.
  • [[ci|CI]] runs the tests and checks and shows a pass or fail mark.
  • The author answers comments by pushing more commits to the same branch, and the PR updates by itself.

When reviewers approve and the checks pass, someone merges the PR. A PR can also be opened as a draft, which says "look if you like, but this is not ready to merge". A good description says what was wrong, how the author confirmed it, which tests prove the fix, what options were considered, and what was not verified.

example.title: Opening a draft PR with the GitHub CLI
example.code:
$ git push -u origin fix/cart-coupon
$ gh pr create --draft --base main --head fix/cart-coupon \
    --title "fix(cart): keep coupon when the cart is reloaded" \
    --body-file pr-body.md
$ gh pr view --web
$ gh pr ready
notes: Sends the branch to GitHub.

stacked-prs.title: Stacked PRs
stacked-prs.short: Pull requests built on top of each other, where each one contains the one before it. They merge in order.
stacked-prs.body:
Sometimes one change needs another change in place first. The second branch then starts from the first branch, not from main. Its [[pull-request|PR]] targets the first branch, so its diff shows only its own change. That chain is a stack of PRs. They merge from the bottom up. When the bottom PR merges, the next one is pointed at main, and so on.

Stacking keeps each PR small and readable while the work builds up. The cost is waiting and upkeep. A change near the bottom forces every branch above it to be rebased, which means replaying its commits on top of the new version.

Not every set of related PRs needs a stack. Changes that touch separate code can each sit directly on main and merge in any order. When you review a stacked PR, check its base branch, because the diff against main would include every PR below it. Each PR's own tests should fail on the branch below and pass on its own branch.

example.code:
$ git log --oneline main..feat/export-csv

7e0b3f5 refactor(export): split row building from writing
2a9c6d1 fix(orders): keep the order date in UTC
$ gh pr create --base refactor/export-rows --head feat/export-csv

code-review.title: Code review
code-review.short: Another person, or a tool, reading a change for problems before it merges, and leaving comments on the diff.
code-review.body:
Code review means someone other than the author reads the [[diff|diff]] of a [[pull-request|pull request]] before it merges. The reviewer looks for bugs, unclear code, missing tests, and changes that break something elsewhere. They leave comments on specific lines. The author answers, fixes or explains, and the reviewer approves once satisfied.

Review works because the author is too close to the code. The author knows what the code is meant to do and reads that into it. A reviewer reads what it actually does.

A useful habit is to check the claims. If the description says "a stuck job no longer blocks the queue", look for the test that proves it, and run it. Another is to trace an edge case by hand, such as an empty list, the 9th job when 8 workers are busy, or two requests at once.

Many projects also run an automated reviewer, a bot that posts comments the way a person does. Its comments still need a human to judge them.

example.title: Reviewing a PR from the command line
example.code:
$ gh pr checkout 1234
$ gh pr diff 1234
$ pytest tests/test_jobs.py
$ gh pr review 1234 --comment \
    --body "jobs.py: with 9 jobs and 8 workers, does the 9th job get its own 30 s?"
$ gh pr review 1234 --approve
notes: Downloads the branch of PR 1234 and switches to it, to run it locally.

ci.title: Continuous integration (CI)
ci.short: A server that builds the code and runs tests and checks on every pull request, before anything merges.
ci.body:
Continuous integration, or CI, means a server builds and [[test|tests]] every change as soon as someone pushes it. No person has to start it. The result shows on the [[pull-request|pull request]] as a green check or a red cross, and a team usually blocks merging until CI is green.

CI catches what a busy person skips. Nobody runs every test on every platform before every push, but a machine does it every time, the same way. It also checks the code in a clean setup, so problems that only appear outside the author's own computer show up.

Common CI jobs run the [[lint|linter]], run the tests on several operating systems or language versions, build the program, and scan for secrets such as API keys committed by mistake. GitHub Actions keeps its setup in files under .github/workflows/. Other services, such as GitLab CI and CircleCI, work the same way.

Green CI means the existing checks passed. It does not mean the change is tested. In review, check that the new tests run in CI and are not skipped.

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install ruff
      - run: ruff check
      - run: ruff format --check
